analysis.one_liner: Makes large data centers pay their full grid-upgrade costs and offers tax credits for new generation and water recycling.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2026 with zero cosponsors and referred to two House committees, the bill has had no further action; Congress remains in session through early January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: As data centers strain the power grid, this bill would change federal utility law so that any customer drawing 100 megawatts or more—data centers, mainly—must cover the full cost of the generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades needed to serve it, instead of spreading those costs across everyone's electric bill. It would also give a 30% tax credit to projects that build extra generation capacity shared with homes and farms, and a 30% tax credit for water-recycling systems that keep data centers and factories from draining rivers and aquifers. States and utilities, not the federal government, would work out the details, and states would only be required to consider the new rules, not adopt them.
analysis.who_benefits: Residential, agricultural, and small-business electric customers, who would be shielded from rising bills caused by data center load growth; communities whose water supplies are protected by recycling projects; and, deliberately, data center and generation developers, who gain a federal framework encouraging their expansion plus substantial tax credits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Household electric customers and data center developers

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a federal standard requiring rates for large-load customers (100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus) to recover the full incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade needed to serve them, including if they later terminate their contract, and requiring financial assurances before upgrades are built [S2].

It directs utilities to consider mechanisms encouraging large-load customers to build or buy new generation sufficient to serve their own load, with any excess capacity made available through long-term contracts to entities serving residential, agricultural, and small-business customers [S2].

It creates a 30% investment tax credit for the portion of new generation capacity that exceeds a covered data center's projected demand (up to 50% of that demand) and is contracted for at least 10 years to load-serving entities, with recapture rules if the data center understates its demand or drops the contract [S2].

It creates a 30% investment tax credit for water recycling projects, including onsite recycling at data centers and factories, replacing freshwater with municipal recycled water, and building or expanding municipal water recycling systems [S2].

The bill's findings state that new large loads can place upward pressure on power costs and that large-load customers should bear the full incremental cost of infrastructure built primarily for them [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who absorb the revenue cost of the two 30% tax credits; data center operators, who would pay more upfront for grid upgrades and financial assurances than they do today; and electric utilities, which face new federal mandates to design rates and run proceedings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, data center operators, and utilities

drawbacks.text: The ratepayer protections are PURPA 'standards,' which states must consider but are not required to adopt; each state regulator or nonregulated utility can complete a proceeding and decline to implement the rules, so protection for household bills depends entirely on where you live [S2].

The additive-generation requirement uses 'consider' language, and the bill expressly says no state or utility can be forced to mandate physical allocation of generating capacity or a uniform set-aside, weakening the guarantee that data centers will actually add generation for everyone else [S2].

The two 30% tax credits reduce federal revenue, and the generation credit rewards building capacity in excess of a data center's needs, which could subsidize projects that overbuild; verification relies on taxpayer certification, engineering studies, and Treasury guidance [S2].

By design, the bill facilitates data center expansion—an 'all-of-the-above' buildout of power and water infrastructure—so total electricity demand grows faster even in states that decline the standards, still pressuring bills and water supplies there [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is genuinely pro-consumer: data centers demanding power on the scale of mid-sized cities would have to pay for the infrastructure they cause rather than pushing those costs onto everyone's electric bill. But the strength of that protection is limited—states must consider the standards, not adopt them—and the bill pairs the protection with tax credits and a national policy statement that facilitate more data center construction, so total grid and water stress keeps growing even where the protections are not implemented.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late June 2026, referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, and has had no hearings, markup, or floor action since; it has attracted no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Baumgartner (R-WA) introduced the bill on June 24, 2026, with no cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Energy and Commerce [S4].
No further action—no committee vote, hearing on the record, or floor consideration—appears in the action history, and the 119th Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one: the bill has not advanced, so data center operators and electric customers continue under the existing rules, with infrastructure costs allocated however state regulators currently allow.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Michael Baumgartner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing large-load ratepayer standards and generation and water-reuse tax credits.

for.name: House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral; neither committee has acted on it in the record to date.

sides.party_line_note: No opposition appears in the record, but no cosponsors from either party signed on, so the bill's level of support is a single Republican sponsor.

industries.industry: Data center and AI computing operators
industries.note: The bill makes federal policy out of facilitating data center development and credits excess capacity they build, locking in their growth; at the same time it requires them to pay the full incremental cost of grid upgrades and post financial assurances, ending a practice under which existing customers could absorb some of those costs. Their interest in this bill both supports and constrains what ordinary ratepayers want.

Utilities gain guaranteed financial assurances from large customers and a wave of ratepayer-funded generation construction, but lose flexibility to spread large-load upgrade costs across the customer base and must run new federal-standard proceedings.

A new 30% investment tax credit for generation capacity beyond a data center's own need, if contracted for 10+ years to utilities serving homes and farms, directly subsidizes capacity that would serve ordinary customers.

The water reuse credit covers building or expanding municipal water recycling systems and replacing freshwater use with recycled water, protecting aquifers and surface water that communities depend on.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action months after introduction, the bill is very likely to sit until the 119th Congress ends without a vote. Its best realistic path is having elements folded into a larger energy or tax bill, since stand-alone ratepayer-protection proposals rarely reach the floor without broader support.
